original_question: Consider selecting $r = O(k)$ uniformly random row indices $I$ and then choosing column indices $~J$ so that $A(I,:) A(I,~J) ~T$. What are sufficient conditions on $r$ and on the kernel $f$ which guarantee that | _~J A - A |_F <= c(n, m, k) | _J A - A |_F with high probability, where $c(n, m, k)$ grows at most logarithmically in its arguments? In other words, when does column selection on a random subset of the rows perform similarly to column selection on the full matrix?
target_in_paper: Problem 4.4 in Section 4.1.3 (“Incoherence and random row subsampling”): the row-subsampled kernel-matrix column-selection question.
correct_elements: Your draft already captures the core of the paper’s target problem: sample r = O(k) rows uniformly at random, choose column indices \u007eJ from the sampled matrix A(I,:), and ask for a high-probability Frobenius-norm guarantee comparing the full-matrix error of the sampled-row column selection against the full-matrix error from a k-column selection on A itself. The final sentence of your draft also matches the paper’s own informal restatement very closely: it asks when column selection on a random subset of rows performs similarly to column selection on the full matrix.
missing_details: The ambient matrix class: A \in \mathbb{C}^{n\times m} with n \gg m.
A is specifically a kernel matrix with entries A_{ij} = f(x_i, \omega_j), where f is generally non-symmetric.
The benchmark set J consists of k column indices for which A is assumed to be accurately approximated by those columns, written in the paper as A \approx A(:,J)T.
The paper compares projection errors \|\Pi_{\u007eJ}A - A\|_F and \|\Pi_J A - A\|_F; \Pi_J must be defined as the projection onto the column space of A(:,J).
The sampled-row column set \u007eJ is obtained by finding a good column approximation of the sampled submatrix, written as A(I,:) \approx A(I,\u007eJ)\u007eT.
The probability is over the uniformly random choice of the row index set I with |I| = r.
The desired growth condition is that c(n,m,k) be at most logarithmic in n, m, and k.

The paper asks for sufficient conditions on r and on the kernel f that are direct and efficiently verifiable from f itself, not merely abstract incoherence/sparsity assumptions on an unknown factorization of A.
The scope is narrow: this is not the full CSSP/RRQR problem of Problem 4.1, but the kernel-matrix row-subsampling specialization in Problem 4.4.
refined_question: Let A \in \mathbb{C}^{n\times m} with n \gg m be a (generally non-symmetric) kernel matrix with entries A_{ij}=f(x_i,\omega_j). Assume that A admits an accurate k-column approximation, i.e. there is a set J of k column indices such that A \approx A(:,J)T, equivalently \Pi_J A is a good column-subset approximation, where \Pi_J denotes the projection onto \operatorname{col}(A(:,J)). If I \subseteq \{1,\dots,n\} is a uniformly random set of r=O(k) row indices and one chooses a set \u007eJ of column indices from the sampled matrix A(I,:) so that A(I,:) \approx A(I,\u007eJ)\u007eT, what direct, efficiently verifiable sufficient conditions on r and on the kernel f guarantee, with high probability over I, that \|\Pi_{\u007eJ}A-A\|_F \le c(n,m,k)\,\|\Pi_JA-A\|_F, where c(n,m,k) grows at most logarithmically in n, m, and k? In other words, when does column selection on a uniformly row-subsampled kernel matrix perform comparably to column selection on the full matrix?
justification: The nearest official formulation is Problem 4.4, not the broader Problem 4.1. Section 4 first defines the CSSP setting and the projection notation \Pi_J, together with the quasi-optimal comparison standard. Section 4.1 then frames the general question of when greedy/randomized column-selection methods work. Section 4.1.3 specializes this to kernel matrices A_{ij}=f(x_i,\omega_j), uniformly random row subsampling, and the exact inequality your draft is aiming at. Your draft’s garbled middle expression corresponds to the paper’s sampled-submatrix approximation A(I,:) \approx A(I,\u007eJ)\u007eT. The refined version restores the paper’s notation, adds the missing kernel-matrix hypotheses and projection notation, and preserves the paper’s emphasis on direct, efficiently verifiable conditions on f.
